uncitedSentences.sentence: Automated written corrective feedback (AWCF) refers here to error feedback generated by software rather than by a teacher or peer, encompassing both dedicated automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems and large language models.

This review synthesises the project library's evidence on AWCF for second-language writing, organised around three themes: detection accuracy relative to established tools, revision behaviour, and learner and teacher engagement.
The library contains no controlled comparison of AWCF against teacher feedback on accuracy outcomes; the evidence is therefore drawn from corpus-based tool comparisons and naturalistic case studies.

content.text: Luo et al. (2025) compared ChatGPT-4 against Grammarly on 30 essays by non-English-major undergraduates at a Chinese university, analysing error flagging across three prompts. ChatGPT-4 maintained high precision across three prompts (94%, 98%, 94%), exceeding Grammarly's 85%, and with the most sophisticated prompt outperformed Grammarly on direct-translation, word-choice, sentence-structure and pronoun errors (Luo et al., 2025). Recall improved considerably across prompts, from 10% to 33% to 55% (Luo et al., 2025). The finding that a more sophisticated prompt did not reliably capture errors flagged by a simpler one further cautions against assuming prompt quality guarantees consistency (Luo et al., 2025). The design offers fine-grained error-category analysis but rests on 30 essays from intermediate-level learners at one Chinese institution, which the authors note limits generalisation (Luo et al., 2025).

uncitedSentences.sentence: Whether learners act on AWCF is a separate question from whether the tool detects errors.

content.text: Whether learners act on AWCF is a separate question from whether the tool detects errors. Naturalistic case evidence suggests that AWE tends to highlight rather than correct errors, whereas teacher feedback addressed more error types (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). The two focal learners differed sharply in resubmission frequency, and the more engaged learner improved more on both feedback sources (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). In a larger classroom case, 88% of 33 students submitted to AWE more than five times (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

content.text: Teacher uptake is uneven: four of six teachers were positive about Grammarly, and no division of labour emerged in which the tool handled lower-order concerns (Koltovskaia, 2022). Reported time savings conflicted with observed feedback distribution (Koltovskaia, 2022). Hyland (2025) argues that ChatGPT's retiring stance leaves it unable to offer accurate feedback on rhetorical and pragmatic aspects of argument. These studies rely on small samples and hypothetical or single-context scenarios; none traces how teacher and automated feedback interact over time in an intact course.
